Moving SVG illustrations out of React and into files

November 13, 2026•code

Every crop in Odlingsguiden has an illustration. A small icon in the lists and a bigger picture on the crop page. The guides have larger drawings too.

All of them were React components. Just SVG in JSX. It’s the obvious way to do it in a React app and it worked fine for a long time.

Then we redrew all of them in a new pen style, because the old ones more or less disappeared in dark mode. The new style has a lot more detail. And a lot more detail means a lot more SVG nodes.

Every shape in the new style is three to five elements. A base, a wash, a lighter wash a bit off to the side, the outline and a faint second pen stroke. That’s what makes it look hand drawn. It’s also why a simple crop like an onion ends up around 35 to 55 elements.

1.2 MB of HTML

The guides are prerendered, so every drawing ended up inline in the HTML. The start page was 1.2 MB. The guide overview 1.1 MB. And React had to hydrate around 3,700 SVG nodes on the start page alone.

One guide drawing was 855 nodes. You don’t really think about that when it’s just a component you import.

Should it be images instead?

My first thought was WebP or AVIF. So I measured all seven guide drawings.

Pixel images only win on small low resolution screens. On retina, which is basically every phone, a WebP at 720 px weighs about the same as the SVG gzipped. At 1440 px, twice as much. And you’d need several widths times two themes times two formats.

SVG is sharp at every size and it’s one file. The bytes were never the problem. The problem was that the drawings were inline, in the HTML and in the hydration. Plain SVG files fix that just as well as pixels.

Drawings as background images

The guide drawings use the page’s colour variables, so they look right in both light and dark mode. A plain <img> can’t read CSS variables from the page.

So the build writes two files per drawing, one light and one dark. The component is just a <span role="img"> with the right aspect ratio, and CSS picks the background image based on the theme. A background image only loads when its rule matches, so dark mode never downloads the light one.

Guide overview went from 1,066 kB to 23 kB.

Icons with <use href>

The start page was still 525 kB. Turns out 504 kB of that was the list icons, 75 of them, inlined by the prerender.

Here I found something I didn’t know. An SVG loaded with <use href> from an external file inherits the CSS variables from the page. So one file per icon works for both themes:

<svg>
  <use href={`${url}#icon`} />
</svg>

The file just has a <symbol id="icon"> in it. All the lazy loading logic I had built for the icons could be removed.

Start page: 525 kB to 66 kB.

The Vite trap

Of course something broke. Vite inlines small assets as data URLs, anything under 4 kB by default. And <use href> can’t read a data URL. So the smallest icons just didn’t show up.

Changing assetsInlineLimit didn’t help. What worked was the ?no-inline query on the import:

import.meta.glob('./icons/*.svg', {eager: true, query: '?no-inline', import: 'default'})

I only caught it because the hydration test logs console errors from headless Chrome, and Chrome said “Unsafe attempt to load URL data:”. Would have missed that one otherwise.

Then the crop pictures too

Same thing for the bigger picture on each crop page. 186 of them, each a React component in its own lazy chunk with loading states and fade-ins. Now it’s a file with a <symbol>, and the prerender adds a <link rel="preload"> for it in the head.

The carrot page went from 169 kB to 110 kB. 337 kB before the icons.

A budget that actually stops me

The build warned the whole time, and I knew it was big. But every way I tried to load the drawings separately made them blink in when the page loaded. So they stayed inline until there was a way that didn’t.

Now there’s a size check that runs when I release, and it stops the release if the index chunk or any prerendered page grows past its budget. Warnings are not enough. A red release is.

And a rule written down for the future: graphics are files.
